evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The database analyzes 𠬝 as an early graph for 服: its oracle-bone and bronze forms combine 又, interpreted as a hand, with 卩, interpreted as a kneeling person, depicting a person being subdued. It reports oracle-bone use as a verb ‘conquer’ and as a noun for conquered people, including sacrificial victims. This is the database’s analysis, not an uncontested reading of every occurrence.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 𠬝 entry

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The database calls 服 a later phono-semantic form of 𠬝, with 凡 added; it says bronze forms of 凡 sometimes became 舟, and later clerical/regular forms account for the modern 月-like shape. It also reports oracle-bone 服 used as a place name and bronze 服 for office or duty, citing 班簋. This supports a proposed graph history, but the page does not resolve the competing tray/service interpretation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 服 entry

evidence.field: 服 entry and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen gives ‘用也’ and an alternative vehicle-related sense, then analyzes the graph as 从舟𠬝聲; it records 𦨈 as an old form from 人. Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary says 舟 here should be 周 in the vehicle explanation. This is an early lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the proposed ancient graph history.
evidence.title: 說文解字「服」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解 / 服; graphic forms
evidence.text: The entry lists one oracle-bone form, eight bronze examples among 33, one small-seal form, and 27 bamboo/silk examples. These establish that the database indexes multiple stages and variants; no glyph image was visually inspected in this research, so individual strokes and graphic transitions are not asserted here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 服 entry

evidence.source: Newton Encyclopedia (Chinese-language character entry; secondary compilation)
evidence.text: This entry summarizes a competing analysis: 服 depicts a person serving at a dish/tray, with 林潔明 cited for the ‘person presenting a tray’ interpretation; another analysis treats the added shape as 凡 ‘tray’. It attributes to 姚孝遂 the view that the form is a tray rather than 舟. It further claims early Western Zhou 井侯簋 retains 凡 and that 大盂鼎 shows a shift toward 舟, with later clerical forms leading to the modern shape. These detailed datings and shape identifications are secondary assertions; the individual inscriptions were not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 服(漢字): 字源解說、詳細字義、古籍解釋

evidence.source: 馮時, 班簋銘文補釋, 清華大學
evidence.text: The article transcribes the Western Zhou Mu Wang-era vessel inscription, dated by the author to the Mu Wang reign, as ‘王令毛伯更虢城公服’ and interprets it in the context of succession to duties/office. The database cites the same line for 服 as office or duty. This attests an early institutional use, not a clothing sense.
evidence.title: 班簋銘文補釋

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Appendix: Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction
evidence.field: Old Chinese/Middle Chinese entries for 𠬝 and 服
evidence.text: In the Baxter–Sagart 2011 reconstruction data shown on the inspected page, 𠬝 ‘subdue; submit’ and 服 ‘quiver’, ‘garment; wear’, and ‘subdue, submit’ are listed with Middle Chinese bjuwk and Old Chinese *bək {*[b]ək}. The same source lists 服 ‘box of a carriage’ separately as bjuwX and *bəʔ {*[b]əʔ}. The matched form supports a phonetic role for 𠬝 in the compound; reconstructions are scholarly models, not direct recordings of ancient pronunciation.
evidence.title: Appendix:Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Appendix: Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction
evidence.text: The listed readings for 𠬝 are Mandarin fú and Middle Chinese bjuwk; the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction is *bək {*[b]ək}, glossed ‘subdue; submit’. This page does not independently identify an original spoken name for any depicted object; no object-name borrowing is required for the 𠬝-as-phonetic analysis.
evidence.title: Appendix:Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The 服 entry gives modern Mandarin readings including fú and fù. Its Guangyun table records 房六 fanqie and a voiced labial entering-tone Middle Chinese category; the reconstructed table identifies 奉 as the initial and 屋 rhyme. These are character readings, distinct from a hypothetical name for a depicted tray or other object.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 服 entry

evidence.text: The inspected page lists Mandarin fú/fù among several readings; Cantonese Jyutping fuk6; Japanese Go-on buku and Kan-on fuku; Korean pok; and Vietnamese phục. These modern or historical reading traditions do not establish the graph’s semantic origin.
evidence.title: 服 - 维基词典

evidence.source: 中文百科全書 (Newton Encyclopedia compilation)
evidence.field: 詳細字義 / cited classical examples
evidence.text: The compilation cites 《詩經·魏風·葛屨》‘好人服之’ for the verb ‘wear/put on’, and 《詩經·曹風·候人》‘彼其之子，不稱其服’ for clothing/attire. It also lists senses such as serving, submitting, administering medicine, and mourning. These are transmitted classical textual attestations; the page does not provide manuscript dates, and the semantic links among them are not established by the gloss sequence.
evidence.title: 服(漢字): 字源解說、詳細字義、古籍解釋

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The entry quotes the Shuowen explanation ‘用也。一曰：車右騑，所以舟旋。从舟，𠬝聲’ and notes that the graph was used as a place name in oracle-bone inscriptions and for duty/office in bronze inscriptions. This separates attested uses from the hypothesized graphic motivation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 服 entry

evidence.text: The entry defines 箕服 as an arrow case/quiver and quotes 《國語·鄭語》‘檿弧箕服，實亡周國’, with 韋昭 glossing 服 as an arrow container; it also notes 《漢書·五行志》’s variant 箕/萁 and 顏師古’s explanation. This documents an old quiver use of the word 服 within compounds but does not establish that the graph originated as a drawing of a quiver or that its sound came from a recoverable object name.
evidence.title: 箕服的解釋|箕服的意思

evidence.text: The file page identifies a modern Inkscape vector redraw of 服 in Shang oracle script style, lists the Academia Sinica oracle-bone font among its sources, and states that the SVG representation is public domain. It is a redraw, not a photograph of an inscribed artifact.

evidence.text: The page identifies a modern Inkscape vector redraw of 服 in bronze-script style and links the image to the B13418 example in hanziyuan.net. It states that the SVG representation is public domain. The file description does not specify a narrower date or bronze tradition.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解 and indexed graphic forms
evidence.text: The entry presents 服 as a later phonosemantic form associated with 𠬝, while also reporting 林潔明’s competing interpretation of a person presenting a tray in service. It says a 凡-like bronze component may have changed to 舟, and later forms came to be classified under 月. The page indexes oracle, bronze, seal, and bamboo/silk forms. This is a source’s account, not settled identification of the disputed component history.

search_audit.outcome: The search did not return a usable 服-specific form record. Inspected the official rights notice and confirmed its CC0 scope for glyph images and glyph attributes obtained through the query interface.

Inspected the oracle file page and its public-domain notice. The bronze file page had already been inspected. A Commons file labeled 服-seal.svg describes 般, so it was excluded. Direct preview fetches returned cache-miss errors; URLs are included as surfaced by the tool, not treated as successful image access.

gaps: No separate primary oracle-bone corpus entry or securely dated oracle-bone inscription was opened for 服 or 𠬝; the database reports the uses, but the individual records and images were not inspected.

The tray/凡 versus 舟 identification is disputed. The claim that a particular early bronze form retains 凡 and that another is a corruption to 舟 is sourced here to a secondary compilation, not verified from inspected inscription facsimiles; therefore origin_relation for 凡 versus 舟 remains uncertain on this evidence.
Shuowen’s graphic analysis is recorded as a historical explanation, not treated as proof that the earliest graph contained 舟.

There is no independently established sound for a depicted tray, boat, quiver, or other object that would support a whole-graph phonetic-loan theory. The shared reconstructed reading of 𠬝 and 服 supports the phonetic-component analysis without requiring an object-name hypothesis.

The 服 ‘quiver’ use is supported in the compound 箕服 and reconstructions, but the earliest independent attestation and whether it is a separate word, semantic extension, or graph borrowing have not been established.

Classical quotations provide attested clothing/wearing senses, but the path from ‘subdue/serve’ to ‘wear/clothing’ is not demonstrated. Chronology should not be inferred from the dictionary’s ordered glosses.
The alleged later 舟-to-月 change is summarized by the CUHK database, but no actual clerical or regular script specimen was visually inspected.
The attempted Shijing primary-text page timed out; its quotations were cross-checked only through a secondary compilation, so manuscript-level dating and textual variants remain open.

No image pixels were inspected in this research. Both proposed Commons images are modern vector redraws, not artifact photographs; the downstream visual inspection should verify what their shapes actually depict.

The Commons oracle file is labeled Shang oracle style, but its page also marks the period as needing specification. Treat its period attribution as approximate and its form identity as a source-provided candidate, not as independent paleographic verification.
The Commons bronze file page gives a general bronze-script label and source reference B13418, but does not establish a more precise inscription date or confirm the disputed 凡-versus-舟 interpretation.
The attempted Commons preview fetches failed with cache-miss errors. The file description pages were accessible and supplied provenance and rights information.
